Chemical Engineering (PhD)
Why Pursue a PhD in Chemical Engineering
UT San Antonio offers state-of-the-art facilities and excellent program faculty, giving students the opportunity to pursue high-level multidisciplinary research projects in the broad fields of health, energy, materials, and the environment.
Graduates of this research-intensive program apply their cutting-edge research to solve problems across traditional scientific boundaries and lead careers in industry, academia, or governmental research laboratories.
Flexible Degree Plan
This degree offers a flexibility not typically found in similar programs to adapt to individualized student interests. Additional courses in leadership and engineering education are offered to complement a variety of future career goals.
Additionally, students in this program are highly encouraged to pursue a semester-long internship in a non-academic setting such as industry, private research institutes, or national laboratories.

Admission & Application Requirements
Applications are submitted through the UT San Antonio Graduate Application. Please upload all required documents (listed below) on your UT San Antonio Graduate Application. It is the applicant’s responsibility to ensure completion and submission of the application, a nonrefundable application fee, and all required supporting documents are on file with UT San Antonio by the appropriate application deadline.
Chemical Engineering (PhD)
Required Degree
Bachelor's Degree from an accredited college or university in the United States or have proof of equivalent training at a foreign institution.
Minimum GPA
3.0 (on a 4.0 scale) Departments may consider GPA of last 60 semester credit hours
Coursework
Completed adequate credit hours or foreign institution equivalent coursework as preparation for the program.
Transcripts*
Required from all institutions attended; international transcripts must be recorded/translated to English
Credential Evaluation
Required if you have earned university-level credit from foreign institutions. Submit an evaluation of your transcripts from FCSA or any NACES-approved credential evaluation agency.
English Language Proficiency
79 TOEFL iBT / 6.5 IELTS / Duolingo 100
For exams taken on or after January 21, 2026: We require a minimum TOEFL iBT score of 4.0.

2 academic or professional reference(s) demonstrating your attributes for successful completion of this program (you will request these through the Graduate Admissions Application; let your recommenders know of your deadline to ensure submissions are on time)

Application Deadlines
Applicants are encouraged to have their admission file completed as early as possible. All applications, required documents and letters of recommendation, if applicable, must be submitted by 5:00 PM U.S. Central Time on the day of the deadline. Deadlines are subject to change.
Chemical Engineering (PhD)
Timing on Admission Decision: Completed applications are reviewed after the application deadline. Admission decisions are released in batches following review committee meetings in early August.

Career Options
UT San Antonio prepares you for future careers that are in demand. The possible careers below are based on data pulled by a third-party tool called Emsi, which pulls information from sources like the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, U.S. Census Bureau, online job postings, other government databases and more to give you regional and national career outlook related to this academic program.
Course Offerings & Schedule
This is a research-intensive program. All courses are offered during the day at main campus. Most courses are offered through face-to-face instruction, but some online course options may be available.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is the focus of the PhD in Chemical Engineering at UT San Antonio?
This program focuses on materials, tissue engineering, electrochemistry, nanotechnology, drug delivery, catalysis, soft materials, microfluidics, polymer materials and more.
What career opportunities are available after earning a PhD in Chemical Engineering?
Graduates go on to pursue R&D positions in different industries, including pharmaceuticals, materials science, energy, food, cosmetics and more. There are career opportunities in academia and National Laboratories as well.
How long does it take to complete the PhD in Chemical Engineering at UT San Antonio?
On average, a PhD in Chemical Engineering takes about 5 years to complete.
Does UT San Antonio offer funding or assistantships for Chemical Engineering PhD students?
PhD students may qualify for research or teaching positions.
In the News
One UT San Antonio researcher is working to make fuel out of thin air (Aug 31, 2026)
UT San Antonio associate professor from the Department of Biomedical Engineering and Chemical Engineering, Gary Jacobs, PhD, is working to convert carbon dioxide (CO₂) into fuel. The process is already an established possibility for a sustainable aviation fuel source, and Gary Jacobs and his team of researchers are working to refine the method. If successful, it’ll be another step towards our society offering more beneficial alternatives to fossil fuel energy.
Read the full story “How one UT San Antonio researcher is working to make fuel out of thin air” to learn more about this ambitious research.
Klesse College professor and project approved for NASA-supported test flight (Sept 02, 2026)
Shrihari Sankarasubramanian, Phd, assistant professor in the Klesse College of Engineering and Integrated Design’s Department of Biomedical and Chemical Engineering, has been approved by NASA for a flight test to advance his research. The research aims to create fuel, oxygen and other chemicals and compounds on the moon and Mars from local resources. Sankarasubramanian and his fellow researchers in partnership with Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) have developed an electrolyzer intended to create these resources from Martian atmospheric carbon. The flight will simulate the gravity on Mars where Sankarasubramanian can properly test the electrolyzer, a major milestone for this research endeavor.
Read the full story “Klesse College professor and project approved for NASA-supported test flight” to learn more about this innovative research.
UT San Antonio engineers turn excess seaweed into a circular solution (Sept 25, 2026)
Researchers at the University of San Antonio are tackling two issues in the Gulf Coast ecosystem caused by sargassum, a golden-brown seaweed, with one solution. Shalinee Kavadiya, PhD, assistant professor in the Department of Biomedical and Chemical Engineering, is working with her team of researchers to address the issues of sargassum overgrowth along the Gulf Coast, as well as the nutrient pollution that causes this excess growth of the seaweed. The project involves using sargassum to produce 3D-printed, reusable filtration models that catch runoff nutrients before they reach the ocean. This project promotes prioritizing sustainability when addressing these environmental challenges.
Read the full story “Into the weeds: UT San Antonio engineers turn excess seaweed into a circular solution” to learn more about this innovative research.
Researchers from SwRI and UT San Antonio collaborate to study solid rocket propellants (Oct 14, 2026)
Researchers at the Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) and the UT San Antonio are working together to better understand solid rocket propellant. By learning more about how the rocket propellant burns, they hope to improve its efficiency and design for defense and aerospace applications.
Read the full story “Researchers from SwRI, UT San Antonio collaborate to better understand solid rocket propellants” to learn more about this innovative research.
UT San Antonio researchers help unlock the potential of peptide catalysts (Oct 15, 2026)
UT San Antonio researchers are working with the Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) to study tetrapeptides. These peptides are formed when four various strings of four amino acids, also known as the building blocks of life, link together. In understanding more about these peptides and how their chemical reactions can be accelerated, researchers are hoping to improve pharmaceutical development, particularly in GLP-1s, which are growing in popularity as a drug used to treat diabetes and help weight loss.
Read the full story “UT San Antonio researchers help unlock the potential of peptide catalysts” to learn more about this innovative research.
